---
title: "Why Dolphin Pods Swell Every Late Summer"
subtitle: "Connecting 6,391 boat sightings to 50+ years of Sarasota Bay life-history research"
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
---

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

dolphins <- read_csv("data/sarasota_dolphins.csv")

monthly_pods <- dolphins |>
  summarize(
    sightings = n(),
    mean_pod = mean(group_size, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_pod = sd(group_size, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
    pct_large = mean(group_size >= 7, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    .by = month
  ) |>
  arrange(month) |>
  mutate(month_abb = factor(month.abb[month], levels = month.abb))
```

When you browse Sarasota Bay's dolphin sightings month by month, a striking seasonal rhythm emerges: groups are smallest in late winter and steadily grow all summer long. Across all 6,391 surveys conducted by the Sarasota Dolphin Research Program between 1971 and 2009, the average pod holds **3.84 dolphins in February**, climbs through late spring and summer, and peaks at **6.02 dolphins in September**—a **57% increase** in group size. By September and October, more than **28% of all sightings** involve large social groups of seven or more dolphins, nearly double February's rate (15.6%).

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 5

ggplot(monthly_pods, aes(x = month, y = mean_pod)) +
  # Highlight the May-July peak calving window reported by Wells et al. (2025)
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = 4.5, xmax = 7.5,
    ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
    fill = "#2a9d8f", alpha = 0.14
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 6, y = 6.35,
    label = "Peak Calving Season\n(81% of births: May–Jul)",
    color = "#1d6f65",
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 3.6
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = mean_pod - 1.96 * se_pod, ymax = mean_pod + 1.96 * se_pod),
    fill = "#264653",
    alpha = 0.18
  ) +
  geom_line(color = "#264653", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(
    aes(size = sightings),
    color = "#e76f51"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 1:12,
    labels = month.abb
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(3.2, 6.6),
    breaks = seq(3.5, 6.5, by = 0.5)
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(
    range = c(2.5, 6),
    name = "Total Surveys"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Bottlenose Dolphin Pod Size by Month in Sarasota Bay",
    subtitle = "Pods expand right after the May–July calving window, peaking at 6.02 dolphins in September (95% CI shaded)",
    x = "Month of Year",
    y = "Mean Dolphins per Sighting",
    caption = "Data: SDRP via OBIS-SEAMAP (6,391 sightings, 1971–2009) | Calving context: Wells et al. (2025), Frontiers in Marine Science"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14)
  )
```

At first glance, you might guess that outsiders swim into Sarasota Bay from the open Gulf each summer. Yet five decades of photo-identification and demographic tracking by [Wells et al. (2025)](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2025.1531528/full) rule that out: Sarasota Bay hosts a tightly knit resident community in which outside immigration is near zero (an annual rate of just **0.003 to 0.013**). Instead, the late-summer surge comes from inside the community itself. Analyzing 482 resident dolphins, Wells and colleagues show that reproduction is sharply seasonal, with **81% of all births occurring between May and July**.

Those newborn calves reshape how dolphins group together across the bay. Resident females—who can live up to **67 years**, begin reproducing around age **9.6**, and nurse each calf over an average **3.5-year calving interval**—gather in warm, shallow seagrass meadows during summer and early autumn to form multi-mother nursery pods. Larger pods provide extra eyes against bull sharks, abundant summer prey, and social learning for calves during their most vulnerable first months of life, before groups disperse back into smaller foraging pairs and trios over the cooler winter months.
